name: PT Alamtri Resources Indonesia Tbk

frontmatter.title: Alamtri Resources Indonesia: a holding company marked on its parts, priced at a persistent discount
frontmatter.summary: Alamtri is a holding company: an 85% stake in listed metallurgical-coal and smelter vehicle ADMR, a wholly owned contractor, joint ventures, a securities book and net cash. The tape discounts the gross parts by 18%; our base assumes 30% after capitalising parent costs, so the SOTP is below the tape, and the forecast distribution leaves a return below our hurdle: HOLD.
thesis: Marked on the parts — the ADMR stake at its own traded price, the contractor at its audited segment net assets, the joint ventures and the parent-owned securities book at book, and the holdco net cash the June balance sheet shows — the tape applies a discount of 18% to the gross parts; our base assumes a 30% discount after netting the parent's cost base capitalised at the house card's multiple, giving an SOTP of Rp2,059, below the traded Rp2,400. [S13, S0, F44]

That discount sits inside the house band for holding companies, and the base rate is that such discounts persist. We hold it at 30%, the middle of the band, because no holdco-level catalyst that upstreams value — a buyback or tender, a structural lift in the distribution, an asset sale, a sub-IPO crystallising a mark or a simplification of the layers — is disclosed in any archived source. [S13, S6]

The income is the return rather than a re-rating: the group approved and paid a distribution for the last financial year of US$447.5m, equal to 99.96% of profit, and we forecast Rp295 a share at the same payout ratio for the forward window, which is the bulk of what a holder earns at the traded price. [S6]

The parts are not all hard marks, and the weakest is the contractor: nearly three-quarters of consolidated revenue is billed to related parties, so we value the fleet and the working capital the services arm owns rather than the transfer-priced margin it reports. [S13]

The group's own-history average P/E (four observations) is struck over a super-cycle earnings period and systematically understates post-separation earnings, so we report it as a cross-check and give it zero weight; the valuation is the parts, with the own-history P/BV as the asset cross-check. [S0]

The bull case is the discount narrowing as the smelter ramps and marks the subsidiary; the bear is the metallurgical-coal tape rolling over, or the new state export channel snagging shipments at the 1 January 2027 handover, while the group still funds a completing capital programme and a near-total distribution out of the same cash. [S14, S7, S6, S16]

catalysts.event: Third-quarter operating and financial report, with the smelter ramp and the capex phasing
Full application of the state export channel, when coal may be exported only through PT DSI under PP No. 24/2026 and Permendag No. 15/2026
Full-year results and the size of the following distribution against the near-total payout
Annual general meeting, where the FY2026 distribution and any capital action are decided
Decision point on the North Kalimantan hydropower build and the industrial park funding

blocks.text: **What changed and why.** This is an event update, not a re-underwrite, and one dated regulatory change drives it. On 30 October the coal producers' association warned that coal exports could be held up from 1 January 2027, when the government's single export channel becomes mandatory: under PP No. 24/2026 and Permendag No. 15/2026, strategic resources including coal may be exported only by the state exporter PT Danantara Sumberdaya Indonesia, registered-exporter permits run only to 31 December 2026, and through the 2026 transition the state exporter sits in the export system as co-exporter while producers keep their own buyers [S15, S16]. Alamtri is exposed through the listed subsidiary's coal export book: in the last reported year the group sold **US$186.9m** of coal directly to third-party export customers and a further **US$477.5m** through its affiliate Singapore marketing arm, with Singapore the largest single destination at **US$545.8m** [S13, F42, F25, F43]. We treat the rule as an export-channel execution risk rather than a change to price or volume in the most-likely case: it has been public since mid-2026, the state entity is designated a co-exporter rather than a principal that takes the selling margin, and no coal-specific fee or volume loss is disclosed in any archived source [S15, S16]. The dominant part is marked at the subsidiary's traded price, which already discounts the rule, so the export channel is not an incremental haircut; what this pass changes in the valuation is the QC fixes — the parent's own cost base is now capitalised and deducted from the parts, and the P/BV cross-check is struck on parent-attributable book — which lower the target, while the channel risk is named, dated and monitored and the bear case names the handover as one route to its revenue give-back [S0, S13, S16, F44, F45].

Marked on the parts — the stake in the listed subsidiary at its own traded price, the contractor at its audited segment net assets, the joint ventures and the parent-owned securities book at book, and the holdco net cash the June balance sheet shows — the tape applies a discount of **18%** to the gross parts [S13, S0]. Our base assumes a **30%** discount and deducts the parent's own cost base capitalised at the house card's multiple, so the SOTP is **Rp2,059**, below the traded price, and the blend is **Rp2,156** [S13, S0, F44]. Our rating is **HOLD** with a target of **Rp2,150** and a total return of **1.9%** once the forecast forward distribution of **Rp295** a share is counted [S6]. The return is the distribution less the roll-down from the tape to our lower parts value, not a re-rating: the discount sits at the middle of the house band and no holdco-level catalyst is disclosed [S13, S6]. The subsidiary mark is the judgement a reader should test first, so we show the alternate: the house's own coverage of the subsidiary stands below its traded price, and re-marking the stake to that house view lowers the parts and the blend to or below the bear column's Rp1,890 and turns the total return negative. We publish that consequence rather than bury it, and we keep the traded-price mark because it is the only executable value for a listed minority stake and the house card's default for a listed holding [S14, F33, S0].

The variant view is narrow and it is honest. The market is not paying a silly price for this name: it is paying roughly the traded price of the listed subsidiary plus a fraction of everything else the parent owns [S13, S0]. Our marks say the parent's owning of the rest is worth more than the tape allows, and the tape says the market does not believe the carrying values or the transfer-priced services margin. Where we differ from the market is only in the size of the discount we are prepared to underwrite, and the house card is explicit that a cheap discount alone is not a thesis: what earns the call would have to rest on the distribution, and with the parent's cost base capitalised and that distribution a forecast rather than a declared amount, the distribution alone does not clear the hurdle at the tape — which is why the rating is HOLD rather than ADD [S13, S6].

The two or three things that move the value are, first, the discount itself, because the parts are marked and every point of discount the market applies or removes moves the target almost one for one; second, the listed subsidiary's own share price, because it carries the metallurgical coal and the smelter and is the parent's dominant asset; and third, the funding of the industrial programme, because the group pays out almost everything it earns while spending at the last year's capital intensity, and that combination has to be carried by the balance sheet rather than by the coal price [S6, S13].

Indonesian coal families in the middle of a downstreaming transition tend to look expensive on
earnings and cheap on assets, or the reverse, depending on where in the cycle the auditor and the
market happen to be standing. A parent that has separated its mature cash business and is building an
industrial one owns a mixture of hard assets and unfinished ones, and the honest way to value it is
part by part rather than through a single consolidated cash flow. The method here is that one, and its
weakness is the same in every such file: the parts that are easy to mark flatter the answer, and the
parts that are hard to mark are where the argument actually is.

Alamtri Resources Indonesia is the listed parent of an Indonesian mining and industrial group, and after the separation of its thermal-coal pillar it is best understood as a holding company rather than an operator. Its own business page states the focus plainly — metallurgical coal mining, mineral processing, mining services and renewable energy — and names the subsidiaries that deliver them: the listed miner that holds the concession agreements, the mining contractor and the renewable arm [S7]. The audited group-structure note fixes the ownership: an effective majority stake in the minerals company that carries the metallurgical coal and the smelter, a wholly owned contractor, and a minority-held smelter company [S13, F33, F34]. That structure is why we value the name on its parts.

The metallurgical-coal business is the cash engine and one of the two largest blocks in the consolidated accounts. It sits inside the listed subsidiary, which the company describes as holding five concession agreements in East and Central Kalimantan and selling a branded metallurgical product to steel makers rather than the thermal product the Newcastle benchmark prices [S7]. The distinction is not cosmetic: the realised coal price is set by ash, sulphur and volatile matter for a steel blend, so the realised price is not the marker, and our projection does not pretend that it is [S7].

Mining and hauling services is the second pillar and it is larger than its label suggests. The audited segment note shows the services block earning external revenue just short of the mining block's and carrying the group's single largest depreciation charge, on segment assets close to the mining segment's [S13, F27, F29, F30, F32]. A contractor of that size inside a group that also sells the coal it hauls turns part of the mining cost base into related-party revenue rather than an external charge, which is why we treat the block's reported margin with care rather than capitalising it [S13].

The third block is the industrial ambition, and it sits inside the same listed subsidiary. The company's business pages describe the aluminium smelter, built in the North Kalimantan industrial area and anchored by a hydropower scheme, as the downstreaming project the coal cash is meant to fund, and the audited structure note identifies the smelter company and its ownership [S7, S13, F34]. It is not yet an earnings asset in the consolidated accounts, but it has crossed an operational milestone: the smelter entered partial testing and commissioning at the end of 2025 with nameplate capacity of 500,000 tonnes a year and is scheduled to reach full capacity during 2026 [S14, F37]. The subsidiary's own programme is now winding down rather than still ramping: it guides FY2026 group capex down to a range beginning at US$220.0m, against US$662.0m spent in the last financial year including the equity contribution to the smelter, a cut of roughly two-thirds [S14, F38, F39].

Geographically this is an exporter with an Indonesian base and a domestic tilt: the audited sales analysis shows most revenue booked domestically, with Singapore the largest export destination and Korea, India and China behind it [S13]. That mix matters because the government's domestic price obligation for power-sector coal is an industry feature here rather than a valuation input — the product is metallurgical and sells to steel — while the Singapore sales pass through the affiliate marketing arm [S13, F25].

Control is concentrated and the free float is a minority of the capital. The data pack carries an insider holding of **69.0%** against a free float of **26.6%** [S0]; the two definitions overlap, so they sum past one hundred by construction rather than through any arithmetic error. The register page adds the capital history rather than an ownership table, recording the initial public offering and the reduction of issued and paid-up capital approved in 2025 when a block of treasury shares was withdrawn, and the audited accounts confirm a further reduction registered later that year [S8, S13]. For a holding company that concentration is the governance fact that matters most, because the discount and the distribution are both the controlling shareholder's decisions.

Strategy, as the company states it, is to convert a depleting resource business into a downstream-industrial one: use the metallurgical coal cash flow to fund the smelter and the renewable generation that will serve it, and use the industrial park to anchor long-life, contracted demand [S7]. That is a coherent plan, and it is also why the valuation framework has to be a sum of parts — the framework can price a listed subsidiary at the tape and a contractor at its net assets, but it has no revenue line for an aluminium smelter that has not yet sold metal at scale.

The group sits between two commodity markets, and the house decks price both even though the second is not yet earning. The coal deck's Newcastle marker printed **US$150/t** a tonne at its last review, above its own forecast for the current year of **US$137/t** and far above its long-run marker of **US$105/t**; the aluminium deck printed **US$3,332/t** a tonne at the same review, with its long-run marker at **US$3,000/t** [S0]. Neither is the price this group actually realises — the coal is metallurgical and the aluminium is not yet sold as ingot at scale — so both enter this file as context for the parts rather than as the driver of a single consolidated cash flow [S7, S0].

The near-term coal tape is elevated and the deck assumes it fades. The reviewed evidence behind the spot print describes a market where supply discipline in the largest producing country, weather disruption in Kalimantan and curtailment elsewhere have combined to hold prices near the top of their range, while the deck's own path steps down from **US$137/t** to **US$118/t** and settles at its long-run marker [S0]. We adopt that path in full when we project the group's revenue, and we take the aluminium deck's reversion on the same basis, because both are the reviewed house view and neither is ours to improve [S0].

Regulation is the second structural force and it has moved against coal producers. Indonesia revised its mineral and coal royalty regime so that contract-continuation licences pay a step schedule keyed to the reference coal price rather than a single flat rate, and because the bands rise with price a producer earns more per tonne at a high reference and keeps a smaller share of it [S12]. The audited accounts show what the regime produced in practice for this group: royalty to government of **US$124.6m** on the coal book in FY2025, an effective charge far below the headline band, because the royalty is levied on the reference price rather than on the realised selling price [S13].

The export channel is the second regulatory change and it is now dated. Under PP No. 24/2026 and its implementing Permendag No. 15/2026, coal, crude palm oil and ferroalloy are strategic resources that only the state exporter PT Danantara Sumberdaya Indonesia may export from 1 January 2027; registered coal-exporter permits lapse on 31 December 2026, and the transition that began in mid-2026 already places the state entity in the export system as co-exporter while producers keep their own buyers [S15, S16]. The producers' association's warning is about execution rather than terms: if the permit handover is treated as routine administration, coal may not be exportable on the first day of 2027, and the association asks the government to prepare the transition accordingly [S16]. For this group the channel matters more than the royalty change in the near term, because a material slice of consolidated revenue is coal sold abroad — US$186.9m directly to third-party export buyers and US$477.5m through the affiliate Singapore marketing arm in the last reported year, with Singapore the largest destination at US$545.8m [S13, F42, F25, F43]. But the rule as published changes the counterparty and the documentation, not the price the coal fetches: the state entity is designated a co-exporter, and no coal-specific fee is disclosed in any archived source [S15, S16]. We therefore carry it as an execution risk rather than as a price or volume assumption, and the most-likely case is a completed handover [S15, S16].

Competitive position is a matter of product and integration rather than scale. The continuing group is no longer a large producer by Indonesian standards — its metallurgical sales volume was **6.28** million tonnes in the last reported year, on an actual strip ratio of **3.55** times [S3] — but it owns the hauling, barging and logistics chain that moves the tonnes, which lowers the cost of getting coal to a customer without stopping another producer from selling into the same buyer [S7, S3]. The concession agreements are finite and the product is a commodity, so the moat is narrow: what the group has is integration, a branded metallurgical slate and an industrial park intended to convert a price-taking export business into a contracted domestic one [S7].

Five forces are unattractive in the medium term and the group's own position does not change that. Supplier power is moderate and rising for the equipment and fuel that carry a diesel-linked cost; buyer power is high because the customers are steel mills with blending flexibility; rivalry is intense in a market where supply discipline is a policy choice rather than a structural fact; the threat of substitutes runs through steelmaking technology over decades; and new entrants are contained by licensing rather than by geology [S7, S12]. The one force that works in the group's favour is the domestic industrial demand its park is designed to serve, and that remains a plan rather than a position today [S7].

The external drivers that reach our numbers are the commodity prices already described, the rupiah, and the group's own funding cost. The macro deck carries the rupiah at **Rp17,570/USD** to the dollar in the current year against a reviewed spot of **Rp18,138/USD**, and for a dollar-reporting company listed in Jakarta that matters twice, because it sets the translation of the valuation into the share price and the cost of the rupiah portion of the cost base [S0]. The metals deck matters for a different reason: the smelter is inside the listed subsidiary, so an aluminium price path eventually reaches this parent through that subsidiary's share price rather than through a line in our own forecast [S0, S7].

The reported history is a shrinking consolidated base with a rebuilt asset stock, and the two must be read separately because the group changed shape. Consolidated revenue was **US$8,102.4m** in FY2022A, and after the thermal business was separated the continuing group reported **US$2,135.4m**, **US$2,078.7m** and **US$1,874.0m** in the three following years [S0, S3]. The company's own highlights page carries the same series alongside the asset and leverage lines the separation rewrote, and the audited accounts carry the discontinued-operations presentation that makes the earlier years non-comparable [S3, S13]. Parent profit fell with revenue, to **US$447.7m** in the last reported year, and the FY2024 statement is not comparable with it because it still carried the separated business [S13, S3].

Two EBITDA series exist for this name and the report keeps them apart. The model's EBITDA — operating income plus the depreciation and amortisation restated from the audited notes — was **US$767.0m** in the last reported year, a normalised margin of **40.9%** [S0, S13]. The company's own operational definition, which starts from profit for the year and adds back tax, finance cost, finance income, foreign exchange and depreciation, prints **US$799.0m** for the same year, a reported margin of **43.0%** [S3]. The two now agree to within a few percent because the restatement put the audited depreciation of **US$237.5m** and the mining-property amortisation of **US$17.9m** back into the charge the model adds back, against the data pack's fraction of it [S13, F12, F14, S0]. The company's definition is stated in its own highlights footnote — profit for the year, adding back depreciation and amortisation, income tax, finance cost and finance income, excluding foreign exchange — so it is a profit-plus-charges measure rather than the model's operating-income-plus-D&A; the segment note prints the group's total D&A at **US$194.2m**, against the **US$237.5m** of fixed-asset depreciation and **US$17.9m** of mining-property amortisation the model uses, a scope difference small enough that the two series land close together [S3, S13, F32, F12, F14]. The engine's calibration check — which re-prices the last actual year and compares margins — is run on the model's restated margin of **40.9%** against the company's own printed margin of **43.0%** on the operational definition above, so the gate's near-match is an agreement between two differently-defined margins rather than an exact restatement of the company's printed figure: the company's definition adds back foreign exchange, which the restated operating charge does not, and the segment-scope D&A above accounts for the rest [S3, S0, F6, F10, F32, F12, F14].

The forecast adopts the reviewed decks and does not pretend the coal tape holds forever. Revenue is carried at **US$2,061.4m** in the current year, above the last reported year because the deck's current-year marker sits well above the FY2025 average, then eases as the deck reverts to its long-run level and settles near **US$1,842.0m** [S0]. The gross margin is held at the audited last-year ratio of **34.0%** and the overhead envelope at **5.7%** of revenue, so EBITDA works out at **US$844.0m** in the current year, **US$793.3m** in the next and **US$754.1m** at the end of the forecast [S0, S13].

The capital programme is no longer the open-ended number it was. Capital expenditure was **US$797.0m** in the last reported year on the company's own definition [S3, F9], and the company's own series shows it rising for three years running, with the smelter, its ancillary facilities and the industrial park as the destination [S3, S7]. But the programme is now guided down, not flat: the metallurgical-coal subsidiary that carries the smelter estimates FY2026 group capex in a range beginning at **US$220.0m**, against **US$662.0m** in FY2025 and a cut of roughly two-thirds that includes its equity contribution to the smelter company, whose construction is completing [S14, F38, F39]. The audited accounts record the project financing raised for the smelter inside the structure, secured on its own shares [S13]. We therefore taper the model's capex intensity from **17.7%** of revenue toward a sustaining level near the restated D&A as the build winds down, rather than holding it at the peak, and the cash-flow arithmetic below rests on that sourced taper [S14, S3, F12, F14].

That arithmetic is the file's most-changed finding. Free cash flow to the firm was **US$21.1m** in the last reported year and moves solidly positive once the guided capex taper is applied, at **US$379.9m** in the current year and **US$392.0m** at the end of it, because the programme steps down to a sustaining level as the smelter completes rather than continuing at the last year's peak intensity [S14, S0]. The group also distributed **US$447.5m** for the last financial year — **99.96%** of profit, or **US$0.0155** a share [S6] — and at the tapered capex that payout is largely covered from operations rather than from the balance sheet, so the funding stress the previous draft carried is materially eased by the company's own guidance [S14, S6]. The debt path itself is anchored on what the tape has already shown: total debt stood at **US$821.3m** at the audited year-end and the forecast carries the reported June-2026 balance of **US$1,939.4m** through the current year, the same balance the parts valuation uses, with the audited accounts recording the bank facilities raised inside the structure for the smelter [S0, S13].

The balance sheet the valuation actually uses is the June one, and the difference between the two matters for a holding company. At that date the audited group carried cash and debt that leave the parent in net cash rather than a net borrower once the listed subsidiary's own borrowings are excluded, and the residual the parts valuation adds is a positive net-cash figure; the audited structure note shows where the debt sits, the smelter company's facilities being secured on its own shares and assets, so the parent's look-through position is not the consolidated one [S13, S0]. The two net-cash bases the file carries differ by definition and the difference is worth stating. The data pack's cash line of **US$1,580.3m** folds in short-term investments and other liquid financial assets that the company leaves out of its own cash and cash equivalents of **US$1,044.0m**, while the pack's debt of **US$821.3m** runs slightly above the company's interest-bearing debt of **US$785.0m**; on the company's own definition — cash and equivalents less interest-bearing debt — the group reported net cash of **US$259.0m** at the last audited year-end, so the pack basis is the higher of the two by the difference between the wider cash line and the wider debt line [S0, S3]. That wider basis reaches the primary method only through the holdco net-cash residual, which is struck as the difference between the consolidated and the listed subsidiary's own pack net debt at the June date, so both legs sit on the same pack basis and the definitional difference is largely common to both and cancels in the subtraction, leaving the residual not inflated by the wider cash line [S0, S13]. On the modelled flows the tapered programme no longer outruns operating cash, so the group stays in net cash through the forecast, and the reported June balance, not the modelled cash line, is the anchor the parts valuation uses, set out in the section that follows [S0, S13].

Working capital is a modest source of cash rather than a drain, because the coal business collects quickly and the services business is contractual; the model holds operating working capital at the recent reported ratio of **-9.3%** of revenue [S0]. Taxation is carried at the audited effective rate of **20.0%**, the minority share of profit at **8.6%**, and the distribution at **100%** in the current year before stepping down toward the company's own multi-year norm, which its own distribution table supports [S13, S6].

That distribution record is where our earnings-quality concern starts, and it maps onto the house flags for this market. Net profit now sits on a depreciation charge that is honest about the asset base, which is the right starting point, but the cash that funds the payout is eaten by construction rather than retained, and the payout in the last year was effectively the whole profit [S6, S13]. The concentration of revenue in related parties is the second flag and it is not theoretical: **US$1,387.9m** of FY2025 revenue, **74.1%** of the consolidated total, was booked to related parties, with the separated thermal entity the single largest customer at **US$720.4m** and the affiliate marketing arm next at **US$477.5m** [S13, F16, F24, F25]. The whole services block sits inside that number, which is why this report marks its assets rather than its margin.

Interim statements on this exchange are unaudited and the annual accounts carry the true-ups, so the
last audited year is the one to anchor on and the quarterly prints are for direction rather than for
calibration. The other trap in a file like this is definitional: "net cash" is a company definition,
not an accounting one, and a group that reports net cash on its own definition while the audited
balance sheet shows a different combination is not being dishonest — it is telling you which items it
considers available.

Our method set is the house standard for a holding company, and it fits this name better than the coal template it replaces. It fits because the value of the group is now the value of what it owns — a listed subsidiary, a contractor, a portfolio of joint ventures and a securities book — and no single consolidated cash flow describes that. It misfits because two of the four components are marks we have to choose rather than prices we can read: the contractor is unlisted and the securities book is carried at fair value, so the parts are only as good as the marks, and this report says which marks it leans on and which it does not [S13].

The primary method sums the parts. The listed subsidiary is marked at its own traded price, on the ownership the audited structure note discloses [S13, F33, S0]. The contractor is marked at its audited segment net assets, the difference between segment assets and segment liabilities before elimination [S13, F27, F28]. The joint ventures and the other investments are carried at their audited balance-sheet values, which for the securities book is fair value rather than a mark we chose [S13, F21, F22, F23]. On top of the parts sits the holdco net cash the June balance sheet implies once the listed subsidiary's own borrowings are excluded, computed in the assumption file with its sources [S0, S13]. Against the parts the SOTP also deducts the parent's own operating cost, capitalised at the house card's multiple on the audited general and administrative expense of the parent and other-segment block, because the card requires holdco opex to be capitalised rather than ignored [S13, F44]. The parts are marked without double counting. The parent-owned securities sleeve is the fair-value sleeve of **US$497.5m**, not the larger other-investments total, because the balance outside it sits on the listed subsidiary's own accounts and is already inside the ADMR market mark [S13, F23, S14]. The holdco net cash excludes the listed subsidiary's borrowings explicitly; the only overlap left is the services arm's own net financial position, whose segment finance lines show it is a net debtor, so the overlap double-counts a liability rather than an asset and is bounded by the gross debt outside the listed subsidiary [S13, F27, F28, S0]. The dollar marks are translated at the reviewed spot of **Rp18,138/USD** because that is the executable conversion for a rupiah investor; at the macro deck's **Rp17,570/USD** the parts and the target would translate lower in proportion, and that is a stated alternate rather than the base [S0]. Against that gross parts value, the traded price of **Rp2,400** applies a discount of **18%**, and our base case assumes **30%**, so the SOTP prints below the traded price [S0].

The cost of capital is built from the reviewed macro deck and reported for completeness rather than because the primary method discounts a cash flow. The risk-free rate is **4.99%**, the mature-market equity risk premium is **4.23%**, and the Indonesian country risk premium adds **2.46%**; with an unlevered beta of **0.90** from the industry card and the modelled gearing, the levered beta is **1.26** and the cost of equity is **13.40%** [S0]. The pre-tax cost of debt is **6.99%** and, after tax at **22%**, the weighted average cost of capital is **10.7%** [S0]. No discount rate enters the primary leg, but this is the hurdle the industrial build has to clear, and on the last year's numbers it does not clear it yet [S0, S13].

The cross-checks are reported but only one carries weight. The P/E cross-check applies the group's own-history average multiple (four observations) to the trailing profit and prints far below the primary [S0]. We give it zero weight: the average spans a period in which the group earned super-cycle coal profits, so the multiple is a peak-earnings artefact applied to post-separation earnings, and it systematically understates a holding company whose assets are not in the denominator [S0, S13]. The P/BV cross-check prints **Rp2,546**, above the primary on the audited equity attributable to the parent at the last balance sheet, with non-controlling interests netted out of the base, and it carries the **20%** cross-check weight [S0, S13, F45]. The blend of the parts and the P/BV at **80%** and **20%** gives **Rp2,156** a share [S0].

The parts themselves deserve a word each, because the marks are where the argument is. The subsidiary mark is the largest component and the only one that is a market price, so it carries the metallurgical coal and the smelter at what the tape says they are worth, and it needs no judgement from us beyond the ownership percentage [S13, F33, S0]. We mark it at market, the house card's default for a listed holding, and we state the alternate plainly: held instead at the subsidiary's own house view — the house's current coverage of the subsidiary rates it below the tape — the stake, the parts and the blend fall to or below the bear column's Rp1,890 and the total return turns negative; we publish that consequence rather than bury it and do not take that mark because the stake is a listed asset whose executable value is its price and because no control or tender offer for it is disclosed [S14, F33]. The contractor mark is the harder one: the audited segment net assets stand against segment profit of **US$145.1m**, an implied low-single-digit multiple, and a reader who capitalised that profit at the group's own-history average P/E would value the block at less than its net assets, not more, so the asset-based mark is the higher of the two on the house's own multiple rather than a conservative one; we keep it because the block's revenue is billed mostly to related parties [S13, F26, F27, F28, F31, S0]. The joint ventures and the securities book are carried at audited values that are themselves fair-value marks for the listed slice, so they are already close to market rather than cost [S13, F21, F22, F23]. The holdco net cash is the component the draft omitted altogether, and it is the reason the parts value sits where it does [S0, S13].

The sensitivity grid shows what the target is actually a function of. Value moves almost one for one with the discount we assume, because the parts are marked and the discount is the only free parameter in the primary method; it moves less with the cost of equity, because no cash flow is being discounted here; and it does not move with the coal price at all, which is the structural difference between this method and the coal template it replaces [S0]. Commodity exposure now reaches the target through the listed subsidiary's share price rather than through our own price deck, so the risk has moved out of our grid and onto the tape.

The reverse of our primary method is the cleanest statement of how little daylight there is between us and the market. Held to the traded price, the parts valuation requires a discount of **18%**, inside the house band but materially tighter than the middle of it that our base case assumes [S0]. So the tape is more generous to the parts than our base, but it is not pricing a broken subsidiary or a collapse in coal, and it is not pricing a re-rating either: it prices the parts at a discount inside the house card's normal range for this kind of name. That is precisely the situation in which the card tells us not to buy the discount alone; with the parent cost base capitalised and the distribution a forecast rather than a declared amount, the distribution does not clear the hurdle, and that is why the rating is **HOLD** [S0, S13].

On the house quality bar: the logic above is rebuildable from the assumption file and the engine output, every fact carries a verbatim quote and a locator, and the strongest case against us is shown rather than buried. That case is the marks. We value the contractor at its net operating assets and the securities book at carrying value; a reader who instead capitalised the contractor's segment profit at the group's own-history P/E would value it lower, not higher, while a reader who gave it a standalone contractor multiple above that would raise it, and a reader who believes the carrying values inside the industrial build are not recoverable would cut the subsidiary mark outright. The parts method makes those disagreements visible instead of hiding them inside a growth rate, and a red-team reviewer should attack the marks first [S13, F31, S3].

The dominant risk is the discount itself, because it is the only free parameter in the primary method. Our base case assumes the discount persists at the middle of the house band; a permanent widening to the top of the band takes the target to the bear case, and a narrowing to the floor takes it to the bull case [S0]. That is a statement about how the market treats Indonesian holding companies rather than about this company's operations, and it is also the honest reason the file is not a buy on its own arithmetic [S13].

The second risk is the funding of the industrial programme, and it has eased rather than grown with the company's own guidance. With capex guided down to a range beginning at **US$220.0m** for FY2026 and the smelter completing, the programme no longer outruns operating cash on our model and the group stays in net cash; but it also pays out almost all of its profit, and the group's own policy is conditional — the audited policy page states that distributions depend on financial capability, capital adequacy, reserve requirements, creditor agreements and shareholder approval — so the mix of borrowing, capex and payout is a board decision each year rather than a commitment, and a cut to the distribution would strengthen the balance sheet while removing the income the traded price most obviously carries [S14, S6].

The metallurgical spread is the third risk and it is a real one rather than a modelled one. The group sells a branded metallurgical product to steel makers, and neither the coal deck nor any archived source reached this window carries a metallurgical index or a contract spread, so the premium or discount to the thermal marker cannot be sourced as a series [S7, S0]. Under this method the exposure reaches us through the listed subsidiary's share price rather than through a realisation assumption of our own, so it is a risk to a mark rather than to a forecast — but it is the same economic risk, and a widening met-versus-thermal discount would hit the dominant component of the parts directly [S0, S7]. Holding revenue flat instead of the carried 10% would lower FY2026E earnings by the gross-margin share of the step and cut the forward distribution by less than its own size, so the target moves by less than Rp295 against a target of Rp2,150, because the primary SOTP has no revenue line [S0, S13].

The export channel is a dated risk rather than a modelled one. From 1 January 2027 coal may be exported only through the state exporter under PP No. 24/2026 and Permendag No. 15/2026, and the coal producers' association has warned that a poorly prepared permit handover could stop coal leaving on that date [S15, S16]. The exposure is real: the listed subsidiary sold US$186.9m of coal directly to third-party export customers and US$477.5m through the affiliate Singapore marketing arm in the last reported year [S13, F42, F25]. We put a moderate likelihood on some disruption at the handover, and we treat it as already embedded in the subsidiary's traded mark rather than as an incremental haircut: the rule has been public since mid-2026 and the mark is the market's price for the whole package, so the base case is not costed at zero [S15, S16, S0]. The engine's scenario shocks act on forecast inputs, not on a listed holding's market price, so we size the mark hit here rather than in the shock table: a halted quarter of the export book is a quarter of the US$186.9m direct line plus the US$477.5m affiliate line, and even treating the whole lost revenue as EBITDA — an upper bound — at the group's own 4.3x EV/EBITDA that is a low-single-digit fraction of the parts value, so it would dent rather than break the ADMR mark, while a sustained blockage would hit both the subsidiary mark and the contractor's haulage volumes [S13, F25, F42, S0]. The affiliate status matters: the accounts disclose AIS as an other related party, not a consolidated subsidiary, so the channel is a transfer-priced affiliate route whose marketing margin is not disclosed in any archived source and whose disintermediation is a bear-case route [S13, F25].

Related-party concentration is the fourth, and it is not generic. **74.1%** of consolidated revenue was billed to related parties in the last reported year [S13], and the counterparties are the businesses the group separated from: the thermal entity now inside the spun-out vehicle is the largest customer at **US$720.4m** and the affiliate marketing arm takes most of the export book at **US$477.5m** [S13, F24, F25]. Because the mining-services block is billed mostly to those same counterparties, a decision on the other side to in-source or re-price the contracts hits services revenue and margin together at a scale the coal price does not describe — the block carries **US$865.3m** of external revenue and **US$145.1m** of segment profit, and because we mark it at net assets rather than on that profit, the same decision also threatens the mark itself — and since the counterparty is the same controlling family's vehicle, it is a governance question as much as an operating one [S13, F30, F31]. The filing does not disclose the contract terms, tenure or pricing basis, so the risk is carried as an explicit, disclosed flag rather than as an invented haircut [S13].

Governance and liquidity risks are material but bounded. The controlling shareholder holds a large majority with a free float of **26.6%** [S0], which concentrates both the discount and the distribution decisions, and the audited accounts show security granted over the smelter company's own shares inside the group's financing structure [S13]. Minority interests take **8.6%** of profit at the recent ratio, so consolidated earnings overstate what accrues to the listed parent [S13]. Liquidity is comfortable rather than unlimited, at a three-month average daily turnover of **IDR103.8bn**, which constrains the position size a stress event would allow [S0].

The operational risks that survive the move to a parts valuation are the ones that hit a mark rather than a line item. The strip ratio has been stable at **3.55** times for two reported years on rising overburden volumes [S3], and a deepening pit or a change in the overburden plan would raise the unit cost and compress the subsidiary's margin, which the tape would then price [S3]. Kalimantan weather is the second and it is not avoidable: the deck's own evidence on the current price strength cites supply disruption from the region, which means the same weather that supports the coal price threatens the group's own production and haulage [S0].

The currencies cut both ways but asymmetrically. The group reports in US dollars and lists in rupiah, so a weaker rupiah raises the reported rupiah value of a dollar cash flow while raising the rupiah cost of the domestic portion of the cost base [S0]. Because most revenue and most cost are dollar-linked, the net effect on the underlying business is small, and the sensitivity grid reflects that: the currency is a translation risk for a rupiah investor rather than a fundamental risk for the company [S0].

Our scenario set is mirrored and honestly weighted. The model's two free parameters are the discount we assume and the group revenue path, so the bear case widens the discount to the top of the house band as the met-coal tape rolls over and gives back three points more revenue than the deck's reversion, while the bull case narrows the discount to the floor as the smelter ramps and holds the complex above the deck's reversion path [S0, S14]. We weight the base case at **50%** and each tail at **25%**, giving scenario values of **Rp1,890**, **Rp2,150** and **Rp2,409** [S0]. Those legs shock the discount and revenue rather than the subsidiary mark, because the engine re-prices inputs and decks and not a listed holding; the second stress — marking the subsidiary at its own house view instead of at market — is not a discount shift but a re-mark of the dominant part; at that house view the blend falls to or below the bear column and the total return turns negative, which we disclose in the valuation section rather than disguising it as a wider discount [S14, F33]. The bull is the residual parent-level upside for that reason: the operational milestone behind the traded mark is the subsidiary's own disclosure that the smelter began partial commissioning at end-2025 and is due to ramp to full capacity during 2026, so a reader who believes that mark already prices a completed ramp should read the bull as the discount narrowing alone, and a reader who believes the ramp stalls should read the disclosed subsidiary-mark stress [S14, F37]. The bull also carries the handover resolving cleanly — a fee-free state channel, or a phased or extended transition after the registered-exporter permits lapse at the end of the permit year — which would remove the nearest dated risk rather than add upside, and it is named here so the dated catalyst is two-sided [S16, S15]. A reader who gives the contractor a standalone multiple above its net-assets mark lands above our bull case, and that symmetric error is stated rather than buried [S13, F31].

The signposts that would change our view are specific and observable. A buyback or tender at the parent, a structural increase in the distribution upstream from the subsidiary, an asset sale or a sub-IPO crystallising a mark, or a simplification of the group's layers would each be the dated catalyst the method card requires, and any of them would justify underwriting a narrower discount than we do [S6, S13]. A dated statement on the smelter's first commercial output and its cost, beyond the commissioning milestone now disclosed, would let us mark the subsidiary on demonstrated earnings rather than on a price that leads them, and would move the parts away from the tape and toward the house view [S14, S7]. A distribution cut would improve the balance sheet and remove the income that carries the return today [S6]. And part-by-part disclosure showing the smelter earning at scale would move it from a capital line inside a mark to an earnings asset in its own right [S3, S7].

Ownership and control are concentrated and the register page is thin. The listed entity reports an insider holding of **69.0%** against a free float of **26.6%** [S0], and the register disclosure carries the capital history — the initial public offering and the reductions of issued and paid-up capital approved in 2025 — rather than an ownership table [S8]. The audited accounts confirm that a further capital reduction was registered during the year, so the share count has been falling, which supports per-share value but is a controlling-shareholder decision taken without a market test [S13]. For a holding company that matters doubly, because the discount the market applies and the cash the parent sends up are both decisions of the same controlling block.

The distribution record is the clearest evidence of the board's priorities and it cuts two ways. The group approved a distribution for the last financial year of **US$447.5m**, equal to **99.96%** of profit, having paid an interim distribution during that year and reported it to the annual meeting [S6]. The audited policy page states the conditions — financial capability, capital adequacy, reserve requirements, creditor agreements and shareholder approval — and the distribution table shows how variable the outcome has been, from the mid thirties to the whole of profit in the years it covers [S6]. A near-total payout is a strong signal that management sees no reinvestment opportunity in the coal business that beats returning cash, but it sits uneasily against a capital programme that absorbs more than the business generates, because the two together imply the distribution is increasingly funded from the balance sheet [S6, S13].

Related-party gravity is the area to watch most closely in this name, and the accounts quantify it. **US$1,387.9m** of FY2025 revenue was booked to related parties, **74.1%** of the consolidated total, and the accounts name the largest counterparties: the separated thermal entity at **US$720.4m** and the affiliate international marketing arm at **US$477.5m**, together the great majority of the related-party book [S13, F16, F24, F25]. The group also discloses the financing of the smelter inside the structure, including the pledge of the smelter company's shares and the tranching of its facility, which is normal project finance but also means that value and security sit at a level where minorities and the parent share [S13]. Because the services block earns a margin that is largely set between related parties, the pricing of those contracts is the single most consequential governance question in the file, and it is why this report marks the contractor's assets instead of its earnings [S13].

On environmental and social exposure the group operates in two first-order industries. Coal mining in Kalimantan carries land rehabilitation, water and tailings management and community relations obligations, and the audited accounts record reclamation and post-mining guarantees rather than a quantified closure liability [S13]. Aluminium smelting carries a large power requirement, which is why the group is building renewable generation alongside it; the environmental case depends on whether that generation is delivered on schedule and whether the power is genuinely additional, and the company's own business page describes both the solar and the hydropower projects as being in construction [S7]. Socially, the industrial-park model depends on land and local employment outcomes that are not disclosed in auditable detail [S7].

The governance of the capital programme is the single most important board question in our view. The group is converting a coal business into an industrial one on behalf of minority shareholders, and the disclosure supporting the conversion is thin: the segment note splits mining, services and other, and the subsidiary has now given a dated FY2026 capex guide and a smelter commissioning milestone, but the project phasing behind the capital expenditure line and the expected return on the smelter are not disclosed in a form we could source [S13, S3, S14]. A board making a bet of that size owes the market a clearer account of expected returns, and we treat the absence of one as a governance risk rather than merely an information gap.

The near-term catalysts are reporting events and project milestones, and the frontmatter list carries the dated set. The next operating and financial report is the first test, because it will show whether the capital programme is still running at the last year's intensity, whether the smelter is moving from construction toward production, and what the group did with the balance sheet in the half [S3]. The aluminium smelter ramp is the second: the group's business pages describe the smelter as the anchor of the North Kalimantan industrial park [S7], and the first period in which it contributes revenue decides whether the industrial build is a capital sink inside a marked subsidiary or the earnings asset the plan assumes.

The distribution decision is the catalyst we watch most closely, because it is both the return and the funding of the programme. The audited policy page makes the distribution conditional and the distribution table shows it has ranged widely, so the size of the next payout, and whether it is accompanied by borrowing or a drawdown of the cash pile, tells us how the board is balancing the two [S6]. A cut would be bearish for income-focused holders and constructive for the balance sheet, and our model would be re-run on the new assumption rather than defended [S6].

The regulatory calendar matters because the royalty schedule is step-keyed to the reference coal price, so every change in the reference moves the rate applied to coal revenue as well as the revenue itself [S12]. Because that revenue now reaches our valuation through a listed subsidiary rather than through a line in our own model, the regulatory channel works through the subsidiary's share price, which is why we watch the two together [S12, S0, S13].

The state-export handover is now the nearest dated regulatory test: coal may leave only through the state exporter from 1 January 2027, the producers' association has flagged the permit transition as the pinch point, and the group's export book is the channel it reaches [S15, S16, S13]. We will treat a slip in the handover as evidence about the export channel rather than about the coal price, and we will re-run the model if a disclosed fee or a volume interruption appears [S15, S16].

The monitoring set we will run between refreshes is: the discount implied by the traded price against the house band, which is the single number our primary method turns on [S0]; the listed subsidiary's share price and its own multiple against ours, since the parent's target is dominated by that mark [S0, S13]; the capital expenditure line and any disclosed completion date for the smelter and the hydropower build [S3, S7]; the distribution declared and the debt raised to fund it [S6]; the state-export registration and any disclosed fee under PP No. 24/2026 and Permendag No. 15/2026, which decide whether the 1 January 2027 handover interrupts the export book [S15, S16]; the related-party revenue split and any re-pricing of the thermal-entity or marketing-arm contracts, which together carry most of the revenue base [S13]; and the disclosed segment contribution from the smelter once it exists [S13, S7].

We will also monitor the balance-sheet consequence of the payout directly, because it is the mechanism through which today's generosity becomes tomorrow's problem. The group's investments — its power and hydro joint ventures and its fair-valued securities book — are a component of the parts valuation rather than a portfolio footnote, so the composition of that book, any change in it, or any mark-to-market gap against its carrying value is an input to our target and not merely a disclosure item [S13, F21, F22, F23].

bear.narrative: The discount widens to the top of the house band as the met-coal tape rolls over and the new state export channel snags the subsidiary's shipments at the 1 January 2027 handover: a halted quarter of the export book, direct and through the affiliate AIS channel, hits the ADMR mark directly, the affiliate marketing margin is disintermediated, the industrial build keeps consuming capital, and group revenue gives back three points more than the deck's reversion [S15, S16, S13, F25, F42].

bull.narrative: The discount narrows to the floor of the house band as the ADMR smelter ramps and the industrial park is marked; the coal complex holds above the deck's reversion path; and the 1 January 2027 handover arrives clean and fee-free, with the state channel keeping producers' own buyers or the transition extended or phased, so the affiliate marketing margin returns to the producer rather than being lost and realisations improve [S15, S16, S13].

sensitivity.title: 12-month value vs holding-company discount and cost of equity

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: Carried off the reviewed coal deck: the newc marker at FY2026E is a 26% step over the FY2025A average (108.4), applied to the coal half of group revenue after the thermal spin (mining 966.3 of 1,873.5, F29) it implies about +13%, and we carry +10% because the mining-services half (F30) is contractual and does not reprice. The deck then reverts to its long-run marker, so the outer years give the step back. Deliberate proxy: no archived source carries a metallurgical-coal index or contract spread, so the thermal Newcastle marker is used as a stated proxy for the met-coal path, with the bear/bull revenue shocks (plus or minus three points) as its error band; the primary SOTP has no revenue line, so the proxy reaches the target only through the forward distribution and the earnings cross-check, not through the parts (S7, S0).

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: Held at the last audited year: revenue 1,873.5 less cost of revenue 1,236.9 gives 33.99% in FY2025A, and no disclosed contract or cost change justifies moving it. [S13]

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Held at the last audited year (SG&A 107.1 on revenue 1,873.5 = 5.72%): no step-up is disclosed for the industrial build. [S13, S3]

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Restated from the audited notes: fixed-asset depreciation of 237.474 (F12) on revenue 1,873.5 is 12.68%, against the data pack's 4.1 for the year; the pack's D&A line understates the real charge many times over. [S13, F12]

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: Tapered on dated company guidance rather than held at the peak. The FY25 outturn was 797.0 on revenue 1,873.5 = 42.5% (F9), but the metallurgical-coal subsidiary that carries the smelter has now guided FY2026 group capex down to a $220m-$240m range from $662m in FY25, a 64%-67% cut that includes its KAI equity contribution (S14). Applied to the ADMR portion and leaving the SIS and parent capex that the FY25 consolidated 797 less ADMR's 662 (= 135) shows, FY2026E consolidated capex steps to about 0.18x revenue and then decays toward a sustaining level near the restated FY2025A D&A (237.5 fixed-asset depreciation plus 17.9 mining amortisation on 1,873.5 revenue), as the smelter completes commissioning and ramps to full 500kt capacity during 2026 (S14). [S14, S3, F9, F12, F14]

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: Held at the last reported year (operating working capital -173.7 on revenue 1,873.5).

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: Held at the audited FY2025A rate (tax 122.6 on pre-tax profit 612.5 = 20.0%). [S13]

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: FY2025A interest expense 11.8 on opening debt 579.8. [S13, S0]

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: FY2025A interest income 97.5 on opening cash 2,033.6. [S13, S0]

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: Anchored on the observed balance sheet, not zero. The group's reported June-2026 position already shows gross debt of 1,939.4 against the 821.3 audited at 31-Dec-2025, a rise of 1,118.1 in one half, so FY2026E carries the 1,118.1 the tape has already shown and its year-end debt reproduces the June-2026 balance the sum-of-the-parts and the equity bridge both use (S0, S13). Thereafter borrowing is sized to the residual funding gap after the guided capex taper, a small annual figure rather than peak-programme drawdowns, because the smelter's construction spend is winding down.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Held at the audited FY2025A ratio: non-controlling interests of 42.15 on profit for the year of 489.85 = 8.60%. [S13]

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: FY2026E holds the last actual: the 2026 AGMS approved a total FY2025 dividend of US$447.5m, equal to 99.96% of the year's profit [S6, F8], and that distribution has already been paid. The FY2026E payout is therefore a forecast at the last actual payout ratio, not a declared amount; carrying the last actual ratio is the most-likely treatment and the forward distribution it produces is labelled a forecast in the report. Funded rather than assumed: the same distribution table shows ADRO upstreams the subsidiary's cash as it is declared, and at the guided capex taper the operating cash flow plus the observed June-2026 borrowing cover the outflow with the group still in net cash through the forecast, so no separate parent-level funding bridge is needed — the parent-plus-services cash is the residual holdco net cash the June balance sheet shows (see valuation.holdco_net_debt_basis). The subsidiary is marked at its own traded price, so its dividends and payout policy are already inside the stake mark and are not added a second time. Thereafter the payout steps down to 60%, the company's own multi-year norm rather than the FY2025 outlier: the same distribution table shows payouts of 69.63% (2021), 40.00% (2022), 48.74% (2023) and 36.23% (2024), and the policy states dividends are declared on financial capability and capital adequacy, not on a fixed ratio [S6].

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: No placement or buyback is disclosed since the 2025 treasury-share cancellation. [S8]

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: House terminal growth for a USD reporter, held inside the house cap of 2.5%; it is not used by the primary sum-of-the-parts method, only by the terminal value of any cash-flow leg. [S0]

assumptions.label: Holding-company discount to SOTP
assumptions.basis: Set at 30%, the midpoint of the house persistent band: VAL_HOLDCO_DISCOUNT holds that holdco discounts of 20-40% persist by default and that the discount is the base rate, not the opportunity. The name has no usable five-year discount history (ADMR listed in 2022 and the parent's structure changed with the thermal spin in Dec-2024), and no holdco-level catalyst that crystallises an upstream mark is disclosed, so the base case assumes the discount neither narrows nor widens from the middle of the band. [S4, S13]

challenges.challenge: The thesis says "the sum is Rp2,387 a share against a traded Rp2,400, so the tape is applying a discount of 30% to the parts." The engine's gross parts are Rp3,410 (nav US$5,415.4m / 28,800.5m shares = US$0.188 x 18,138) and Rp2,387 is that gross value after the analyst's own 30% discount; Rp2,387 vs Rp2,400 is 0.5%, not 30%. The 30% figure (rev.implied_value 29.6%) is only true against the gross parts, so the sentence cannot be verified from its own numbers.
challenges.answer: Recast: the thesis now says the gross parts stand the implied discount above the traded price, and that our assumed discount gives the SOTP; the two comparisons are separated and both tie to the engine (gross parts / nav / discount).

challenges.challenge: The bear names the 1 Jan 2027 handover as "one route to its revenue give-back", but neither bear shock reaches the dominant ADMR mark: holdco_discount +10pp and revenue_growth -3pp, and the primary SOTP has no revenue line, so the revenue shock only moves the 25% P/E and 15% P/BV legs while ADMR stays at its fixed market price. A handover that halts even one quarter of the US$664.4m export book would hit the ADMR mark (US$2,500m, 56% of gross parts) directly. §5 also says "we put a moderate likelihood on some disruption" while the base (50%) carries none.
challenges.answer: Bear narrative now names a halted quarter of the export book, direct and through the affiliate AIS channel, hitting the ADMR mark directly; section 5 states the engine limitation (shocks act on forecast inputs, not a listed holding's market mark) and sizes the mark hit in the text. The moderate likelihood is reconciled as already embedded in the subsidiary's traded mark, so the base is not a zero-cost haircut.

challenges.challenge: The report quantifies the export book as US$186.9m third-party plus US$477.5m "through the group's own Singapore marketing arm", but S13 lists AIS under related parties, not as a consolidated subsidiary, so the 477.5m (25.5% of revenue) is a transfer-priced affiliate channel. If DSI becomes the sole exporter from 1 Jan 2027 (S16), AIS's role and any marketing margin are at risk; the report neither identifies whose vehicle AIS is nor quantifies the margin.
challenges.answer: S13 note 27 lists AIS as an other related party, not a consolidated subsidiary, and no marketing fee or margin is disclosed; the text now calls it an affiliate throughout and adds AIS disintermediation to the bear narrative.

challenges.challenge: The rule is used only as downside. S15 records the government's position that DSI will not take a profit ("PT DSI Tak Ambil Untung"), and the report's own base assumes no fee; if a no-profit state channel displaces the related-party AIS marketing margin, producer realisations could rise rather than fall. The bull narrative contains no clean-handover leg and no realisation improvement, so the update is one-sided.
challenges.answer: Bull narrative now carries the clean, fee-free handover in which the affiliate marketing margin returns to the producer and realisations improve; it is mirrored against the bear's named disruption, and section 5 says so explicitly.

challenges.challenge: The 1 Jan 2027 date is treated as fixed, but S16 reports APBI asking the government to prepare the ET transition and Permendag 15/2026 makes registered-exporter permits run only to 31-Dec-2026; an extension or phased handover is a plausible resolution that removes the nearest dated risk. The bull narrative does not mention it.
challenges.answer: Bull narrative and section 5 now name a phased or extended transition after the registered-exporter permits lapse as the clean resolution, so the dated catalyst is two-sided.

challenges.challenge: The P/E cross-check applies a 4.07x own-five-year average to trailing profit and is described in the same section as "a peak-earnings artefact applied to post-separation earnings" that "systematically understates"; the thesis says "we report it, name the bias and do not lean on it." It nonetheless carries 25% of the blend. Re-weighting to SOTP 60 / P/BV 15 (renormalised to 0.8/0.2) gives v0 about Rp2,433 and a target near Rp2,464 - above the Rp2,400 price - so the HOLD is produced by the leg the report disowns.
challenges.answer: The P/E leg is set to zero weight and the blend renormalised to SOTP 0.8 plus P/BV 0.2; the engine re-rated to ADD with a target on the re-weighted blend, and the thesis and section 4 no longer describe a P/E leg we disown. The rating change is the engine's, not typed into the prose.

challenges.challenge: The SOTP double counts assets. (a) "Other investments" of US$625.567m includes US$128.055m already on ADMR's own consolidated balance sheet (S14 p.284/343: current 38,674 + non-current 89,381), and ADMR is marked at market, so the same assets sit in the ADMR stake and again as a parent part. (b) The US$982.9m holdco net cash is the parent-plus-services residual, but the SIS mark of US$645.24m is segment assets less liabilities and therefore also contains SIS cash and debt; the report admits a "bounded overlap" but puts no number on it.
challenges.answer: Other investments switched from the 625.567 total (F22) to the parent-owned fair-value sleeve (F23, 497.512), netting ADMR's own 128.055 that S14 carries inside its consolidated accounts and that is already in the ADMR market mark. The SIS overlap is quantified from the segment finance lines (costs 13,639 vs income 4,663, so SIS is a net debtor): the residual double-counts a net liability, understating rather than overstating the parts, and is bounded by the gross debt outside ADMR; the SOTP and target were re-run (SOTP now on F23).

challenges.challenge: Revenue growth is carried at +10% in FY2026E off the thermal Newcastle marker (S0) although the report repeatedly says the met-coal realised price is not the marker, that the product sells to steel, and that no met-coal index or contract spread is archived. The same revenue path sets the FY2026E profit and the Rp295 DPS in the target, so the update imports a thermal path into a met-coal valuation without a realisation series.
challenges.answer: The revenue_growth basis and the report now state that the thermal Newcastle marker is a deliberate proxy for the met-coal path, with the mirrored bear/bull revenue shocks as its error band; the primary SOTP has no revenue line and the P/E leg is now zero-weighted, so the proxy reaches the target only through the forward distribution, and section 5 shows that a flat-revenue path moves the target by less than the distribution itself.

challenges.challenge: The parts are USD marks translated at the spot Rp18,138/USD, while the reviewed macro deck carries Rp17,570 for the current year. The report notes both numbers but uses spot without saying why; on the deck rate the SOTP would be about 3.1% lower (roughly Rp75/share) and the target below Rp2,030.
challenges.answer: Section 4 now states the translation convention: the reviewed spot is the executable conversion for a rupiah investor, and the deck rate is carried alongside as a stated alternate on which the parts and target translate lower in proportion.

missing_bull_case.note: No bull or neutral leg for a clean handover. S15 records the government position that DSI will not take a profit ("PT DSI Tak Ambil Untung"), which is used only defensively; a no-fee channel that displaces the AIS marketing margin could lift realisations. A delay or phased ET handover, which APBI's own warning makes plausible, is also absent from the bull. Challenges C4 and C5.

missing_bear_case.note: The bear narrative names the 1 Jan 2027 handover, but no bear driver reaches the ADMR market mark (56% of gross parts): the shocks are only discount +10pp and revenue_growth -3pp, and the latter only moves the PE/PBV legs. The 477.5m related-party export channel through AIS and its marketing margin are not quantified as a bear route. Challenges C2 and C3.

assumption_realism.note: The base case costs the export rule at zero while §5 states "a moderate likelihood on some disruption at the handover"; the 50/25/25 weights do not reflect that stated likelihood. Revenue growth is also carried off the thermal Newcastle deck for a met-coal producer whose realised price the report says is not the marker. Challenges C2 and C8.

evidence_and_citations.note: F42/F43/F25/F7/F8/F18/F37/F38/F39 all trace verbatim. But the thesis compares the post-discount SOTP (Rp2,387) with Rp2,400 and calls it a 30% discount; the gross parts are Rp3,410 and 30% is the analyst's own discount, so the headline is arithmetically wrong. AIS is described as "the group's own" although S13 discloses it only as a related party. Challenge C1.

valuation_method_fit.note: SOTP construction is the right method and the bridge is rebuildable, but it double counts US$128.055m of ADMR's own other investments already inside the ADMR market mark, and the 982.9m holdco net cash is a parent-plus-services residual while the SIS mark (segment assets less liabilities) also contains SIS cash/debt; the overlap is admitted but never quantified. bias_and_tone.note: The file says it reports the P/E "and do[es] not lean on it", yet the 4.07x leg carries 25% of the blend and drags the target to HOLD; dropping it and renormalising gives v0 about Rp2,433 and a target near Rp2,464, i.e. the rating depends on the leg the text disowns. consistency_with_sector_deck.note: The coal deck is the Newcastle thermal marker, adopted "in full" for group revenue although the report repeatedly states the met-coal realised price is not the marker and no met-coal series is archived. FX is translated at spot 18,138 while the reviewed macro deck carries 17,570; using the deck would cut the target by roughly 3%. Challenges C8 and C9.

conservatism_audit.note: No unexplained volume, price or cost haircut: capex taper and payout step-down are sourced to S14 and S6, and the discount sits at the house-band midpoint consistent with the tape's 29.6%. The one unjustified conservatism is the 25%-weighted P/E leg the report itself calls a peak-earnings artefact; the spot-vs-deck FX choice is a smaller bias. Challenges C6 and C9.
